messages.subject: Question about vectorizing
parts:
Hello there,

I've received some excellent help from this list, and now that my code is working - I need to get it to run more quickly. I have read a lot about vectorizing and I've looked up some examples, but I'm having difficulty vectorizing loops like what follows:

for (p in 1:P) {
   mup[p] ~ normal(mum[imodel[p]] + if_else(kc1[p], bkc1,  noval) + if_else(kc2[p], bkc2, noval) + if_else(kc3[p], bkc3, noval) + if_else(kc4[p], 
                            bkc4, noval), sigmap[p]);
    }

I thought that I should be able to do something like the following:

   mup[p] ~ normal(mum[imodel] + if_else(kc1, bkc1,  noval) + if_else(kc2, bkc2, noval) + if_else(kc3, bkc3, noval) + if_else(kc3, 
                            bkc4, noval), sigmap);
 
But I received several error messages about ill-formed equations.

The above mup[p] follows a normal distribution with a mean vector that contains an intercept (this is a hierarchical construction) and a number of fixed effects (so I've used the if_else construction as opposed to multiplying matrices).

Right now, mup, kc1-4, and sigmap are all defined similarly, P-length vectors, e.g. vector [P] mup;. and bkc1-4 are defined as real values, and "noval" is transformed data, because when I simply had "0" in the same place, I received an error message that the quantity had to be a real number, so noval (no value) is defined as real, and is equal to zero.

Any suggestions for how to vectorize this would be greatly appreciated. I can't seem to find an example that I can work from - though maybe that's because I don't know what I'm looking for?

Thank you so much.

Shauna

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Question about vectorizing
parts:
The if_else function isn't vectorized; all the legal signatures
(argument types and return type) are in the index of the manual.

It's worthwhile to do this:

{
vector[P] nu;
for (k in 1:P)
nu[k] <- mum[imodel[k]] + if_else(kc1, bkc1, noval) ...;
mu ~ normal(nu, sigmap);
}

The if_else is definitely more efficient than multiplying by 0 or 1.

But there's much less to be gained compared to when the scale
is a scalar rather than a vector itself. How are you estimating
sigmap[p] here? You can't usually have a different scale for each
observation.

- Bob

Will do:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1868#issuecomment-219460909

I'll try to add this discussion:

Efficiency involves two issues in Stan, and both stem
from first principles:

1. Statistical Efficiency. This is all about posterior curvature
in Stan. Some posteriors are easy to move around than others and
changing parameterizations can help.
(This is also true of Gibbs and Metropolis, by the way.)

2. Computational Efficiency. This is all about efficient
derivatives, and the smaller the resulting expression graph,
the faster the derivatives. That's why vectorization involving
parameters gives you an efficiency boost but vectorization of
constants doesn't.

The if_else stems from point 2 --- there are fewer terms in
the expression graph for the if_else. But there's a catch.
The if_else evaluates both sides, so in general, a conditional
is required, so instead of

a <- a + if_else(cond, b, c)

where b and c are complex expressions, it's more efficient
to do this

if (cond)
a <- a + b;
else
a <- a + c;

We're adding a ternary operation that'll avoid the eager evaluation
of the RHS terms.

- Bob

On Monday, May 16, 2016 at 11:09:52 AM UTC-4, Shauna Sweet wrote:
So if I understand your suggestion fully: I should retain the loop, but within the model statement I should separate the calculation of the mean of the mean (which includes a grand mean of sorts and also a series of fixed effects), from the specification of the distribution of that mean.

In this case, yes. You don't need to do that if the calculation of the mean of the mean can itself be vectorized easily, 
but in your case you'll probably need to do that if you want to vectorize. If I understand your situation correctly then 
you'll want to get it into the form

mup ~ normal(mup_mean, mup_sd), 

where mup_mean is a vector/array of means and mup_sd is a vector/array of standard deviations (of the same length as mup_mean). 
If you have to construct those vectors in a loop that's fine as long as the call to normal is vectorized (that's where the real speedup is).

Hope that helps, 

Jonah
